players.product: large-megawatt diesel and gas backup generator sets (with in-house Enercon enclosures/packaging) for hyperscale and colocation data centers

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results: overall net sales decreased 12% versus the prior year to $1.1 billion as a soft outage environment hit home standby and portable generator shipments, while C&I product sales increased 10% to $400 million (vs $363 million), with core growth primarily from products sold to data center customers both domestically and internationally, including continued international shipments and Generac's initial large megawatt generator sales in the domestic market. Adjusted EBITDA was $185 million or 17% of net sales (vs $265 million or 21.5%). International core total sales rose 5%, primarily on data center products and controls, with a record 16.1% International segment adjusted EBITDA margin.
quarterly_data.figure: net sales $1.1 billion (decreased 12%); C&I product sales $400 million (increased 10%); adjusted EBITDA $185 million or 17% of net sales

quarterly_data.signal: Data center backlog has grown to approximately $400 million on additional orders from co-locators and developers, even after shipments began in Q4 and early Q1 ('good order flow again over the last 90 days'); the majority is expected to ship in 2026. The CEO said the backlog holds only 'a couple of units' for hyperscaler pilot programs and is 'without any material hyperscale business at this point', and contains none of Generac's traditional (non-data-center) large megawatt products. Management expects order intake to accelerate over the next several quarters as data center customers move through qualification and contract stages, and calls 2026 an inflection point for Generac in this end market.

Hyperscalers: Generac progressed to the pilot phases with 2 specific hyperscale customers and is in 'deep negotiations' with both; the pilots run test scripts in Generac's laboratories and at real sites ('in the wild'). With successful completion around the end of the first quarter/beginning of the second quarter, management expects to sign a longer-term master supply agreement with each, after which purchase orders would flow into backlog. One potential customer is sharing specific site build-outs so Generac can match its regional manufacturing capacity to construction (logistics cost and time); with the other 'it's all about, hey, how many slots can reserve for us'. Conversations center on how much Generac can supply in 2027 and 2028 and possibly 2026; hyperscaler supply in 2026 is not in the guide (potential upside). The CEO: 'They need additional supply desperately.'
quarterly_data.figure: 2 hyperscale customers in pilot phase; volumes discussed for 2027 and 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity: Generac bought an existing manufacturing facility in Sussex, Wisconsin in December (faster than building greenfield), coming online in the second half of the year; with it and other tweaks, domestic manufacturing capacity for large megawatt generators is expected to surpass $1 billion by the fourth quarter of this year, plus 'a couple of hundred million of additional capacity outside the U.S.' (a previously cited $500 million was global capacity), which Generac is also looking to expand. The CEO said the $1 billion 'would not be enough' if hyperscaler purchase orders land, and that he would take greater comfort doubling capacity again (e.g. to $2 billion) with hard orders in hand; this first step was taken without orders. A capacity update was promised for the March 25 Investor Day.
quarterly_data.figure: domestic large megawatt capacity to surpass $1 billion by the fourth quarter; a couple of hundred million outside the U.S.

quarterly_data.signal: Competition and supply chain: the large megawatt diesel backup market has seen no new participants other than Generac's entry, which the CEO attributes to the limited number of high-horsepower diesel engine manufacturers (heavy R&D and tooling investment). Generac's engine partner 'has invested very heavily in capacity', so Generac does not expect near-term capacity limitations; the rest of the supply chain (alternators, cooling packages, steel base frames, diesel tanks, and packaging structures typically handled by third-party companies) is being deepened for higher volumes. Management expects Generac's lead times to remain shorter than the rest of the market at least for the near term and 'probably all of 2027', while competitors are 'out kind of 2 years on deliveries', constrained largely by engine supply, 'arguably the most critical component in the gen set'.
quarterly_data.figure: competitors out kind of 2 years on deliveries

quarterly_data.signal: Market sizing: the CEO said the data center market for large megawatt diesel backup generators 'could be as much as $15 billion a year alone', and described Generac's traditional (non-data-center) market for these large megawatt products as 'another, call it, $3 billion to $4 billion'. Generac is a 10% to 15% share player in the North American C&I market and sees about 10% as a reasonable data center share, which would let it double what 'effectively was a $1.5 billion business last year in C&I' in the next 3 to 5 years. The CEO later said that doubling target 'was really a landing on hyperscaler' (one hyperscaler win), with anything higher gated by capacity and supply chain. The traditional large megawatt products launched after the data center-focused sets and are only now being quoted.
quarterly_data.figure: TAM as much as $15 billion a year; 10% to 15% share; $1.5 billion C&I business to double in the next 3 to 5 years

quarterly_data.signal: Data center margins: the CFO said Generac is seeing 'around mid-teens EBITDA margins or contribution margins' on data center projects in 2026 given capacity start-up costs, and 'more high teens margins in the 27%, 28% range' (as transcribed) as it ramps and gains scale, pretty close to corporate average EBITDA margins. The CEO sees further margin upside from bringing more of the package in-house (vertical integration via M&A or organic investment), though not diesel engines.
quarterly_data.figure: mid-teens EBITDA margins in 2026, high teens with scale

quarterly_data.signal: Initial 2026 outlook: consolidated net sales to increase at a mid-teens rate; C&I product sales growth in the plus 30% range, primarily driven by products sold to data center customers, with the Allmand acquisition contributing about 1/4 of the growth and modest organic growth in traditional C&I; no hyperscaler supply for 2026 is in the guide. Q1 2026 net sales expected up 11% to 13%, partly on significantly higher revenue from data center customers. Full-year gross margin 38% to 39%; adjusted EBITDA margin approximately 18% to 19% (vs 17% in 2025); capex approximately 3.5% of net sales to add capacity, particularly for C&I products; free cash flow approximately $350 million.
quarterly_data.figure: C&I product sales plus 30% range; adjusted EBITDA margin 18% to 19%; capex 3.5% of net sales; free cash flow approximately $350 million

quarterly_data.signal: Co-locators: with hyperscaler contracts not yet signed, co-locators are Generac's current data center focus and where it got its first traction; Generac is listed as the preferred supplier with 2 co-locators, making it one of the primary backup power suppliers for their sites around the world, which helps balance reliance on any one customer, though hyperscalers are expected to have an outsized impact given the capital they deploy.

Behind-the-meter gas: spark-ignited reciprocating gas engines are being used to power data centers where grid interconnect is not available and gas-turbine lead times are too long, but in lean-burn prime-power configuration they take minutes to reach full power, so the CEO says 'they're not great pure backup assets'; customers still put diesel backup generators on those sites and plan to move the gas machines to new sites once the grid is connected, so management says this does not shrink the TAM for backup diesel generators ('you need both').
